subject: Biotechnology
title: Virus-Resistant Crops
description: A short lesson to help you apply Virus-Resistant Crops.

hook.text: Papaya ringspot virus nearly destroyed Hawaii's papaya industry — a transgenic papaya saved it.

buildup.text: The Rainbow papaya carries a viral coat protein gene — it triggers RNA silencing against the invading virus.

discovery.text: Pathogen-derived resistance uses the virus's own genes against it — a molecular vaccination for plants.

twist.text: Cassava mosaic virus threatens food security for 800 million people — virus-resistant cassava is in development.

climax.text: RNA interference now protects crops against multiple viruses simultaneously — broad-spectrum plant immunity.

punchline.text: Turn the virus's coat into a shield — transgenic resistance saves harvests.

quiz.question: How does pathogen-derived resistance protect plants?
options: It strengthens plant cell walls to physically block virus entry
A viral gene expressed in the plant triggers RNA silencing against the invading virus
It produces antibodies that neutralize the virus in the soil

details.summary: Virus-resistant crops are engineered using pathogen-derived resistance, where viral coat protein genes or RNA sequences are expressed in the plant to trigger immune-like defenses. The Rainbow papaya, saved from ringspot virus devastation in Hawaii, is the iconic success story.
details.whyItMatters: Plant viruses cause billions of dollars in crop losses annually and have no chemical treatments. Engineering resistance is often the only solution, as demonstrated by the Rainbow papaya that rescued Hawaii's entire papaya industry from collapse.
takeaways: Expressing viral coat protein genes triggers resistance in transgenic plants
RNA silencing provides broad-spectrum virus resistance in engineered crops
Rainbow papaya saved the Hawaiian papaya industry from devastating virus

faq.question: How does the Rainbow papaya resist ringspot virus?
faq.answer: Rainbow papaya expresses the coat protein gene of papaya ringspot virus, which triggers RNA silencing that degrades incoming viral RNA before infection can establish. It has maintained resistance for over 25 years in commercial production in Hawaii.

faq.question: Why can't viruses be controlled with chemicals like bacteria and fungi?
faq.answer: Viruses replicate inside plant cells using the cell's own machinery, making it impossible to target them without destroying the host cell. There are no antiviral sprays for plants. Prevention through resistance, clean planting material, and vector control are the only options.
